title: Sigma and pi bonds
keyIdea: A σ (sigma) bond forms when two orbitals overlap end-on, so the shared electrons sit on the axis between the nuclei. A π (pi) bond forms when two parallel p orbitals overlap sideways, so its electrons sit above and below the axis. A single bond is one σ; a C=C double bond is one σ plus one π; a triple bond is one σ plus two π. Twisting a C=C pulls the p orbitals out of line and breaks the π bond, so C=C cannot rotate. The π bond is weaker than σ and its electrons are exposed, which is why alkenes react at the double bond.

kid: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Each atom lends an orbital. The bond forms where the two orbitals overlap. How they overlap gives two kinds of bond.

If the orbitals meet head on, along the line between the nuclei, you get a σ bond. Its electrons sit on that line. Two s orbitals do this. So do an s and a p, or two p orbitals that point at each other. Every single bond is one σ bond.

Now take two p orbitals that stand side by side, both at right angles to the bond. They overlap above the line and below it. That is a π bond. It is one bond in two parts. A C=C double bond is one σ bond plus one π bond. A triple bond is one σ plus two π.

Try to twist one end of a C=C. The p orbitals turn out of line, and the overlap drops. At 90 degrees it is gone. So C=C cannot turn unless the π bond breaks. The π bond is also weaker than the σ bond, and its electrons are out in the open. That is where alkenes react.
adult: This topic, for ages 16 to 18, explains bonds by the way orbitals overlap. End-on (axial) overlap gives a σ bond with electron density on the internuclear axis. Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a π bond with density in two regions, above and below the axis. Learners use it to explain the C=C bond, its lack of rotation and its reactivity.

The numbers come from mean bond enthalpies: C–C is about 347 kJ/mol and C=C about 612 kJ/mol. Taking the σ part of C=C as roughly a C–C bond, the π part is about 265 kJ/mol, so C=C is less than twice C–C. Sideways overlap is smaller than end-on overlap, which is why the π bond is weaker.

Common mistakes: calling a double bond two σ bonds; drawing a π bond as two separate bonds because it has two lobes; forgetting that every C–H bond is σ when counting; and thinking the σ bond breaks when C=C twists. The σ bond is symmetric round the axis, so rotation leaves it intact. It is the π overlap that is lost.

This idea links to E/Z isomers, which exist because C=C is locked, and to electrophilic addition. The exposed π electrons attract electrophiles such as bromine, so alkenes add across the double bond, while alkanes with only σ bonds do not.

familyTip: Hold two pens tip to tip for a σ bond, then side by side for a π bond. Twist one pen and see how the side-by-side contact is lost while tip-to-tip stays put.

practice.prompt: Two orbitals overlap end-on, along the line between the nuclei. What kind of bond forms?
practice.hint: Where is the shared electron density: on the axis or beside it?
practice.explain: End-on overlap puts the electron density on the axis between the nuclei: a σ bond.

practice.prompt: An alkene has {n} carbon atoms and one C=C, formula CₙH₂ₙ. How many σ bonds does it have?
practice.hint: Count the C–C links (n − 1) and the C–H bonds (2n). Each link has exactly one σ.
practice.explain: There are {=n-1} carbon–carbon links and {=2*n} C–H bonds, each with one σ: {=3*n-1} σ bonds. The double bond adds one π.

practice.prompt: Why can the C=C bond in but-2-ene not rotate at room temperature?
choices: Turning it would break the σ bond
Turning it moves the p orbitals out of line and breaks the π bond
The carbon atoms are too heavy to turn
practice.hint: Which bond depends on the p orbitals staying parallel?
practice.explain: The σ bond is symmetric round the axis, so twisting does not affect it. The π bond needs parallel p orbitals; at 90° its overlap is zero.

practice.prompt: A molecule has {a} C=C double bonds and {b} C≡C triple bonds. How many π bonds does it have in total?
practice.hint: Each double bond has one π. Each triple bond has two π. Single bonds have none.
practice.explain: {a} double bonds give {a} π, and {b} triple bonds give {=2*b} π: {=a+2*b} π bonds in total.

practice.prompt: C–C is 347 kJ/mol and C=C is 612 kJ/mol. About how strong is the π part of C=C?
choices: About 347 kJ/mol, the same as σ
practice.hint: Take away the σ part from the whole double bond.
practice.explain: 612 − 347 ≈ 265 kJ/mol. That is less than 347, so the π bond is weaker than the σ bond.

pool.prompt: Where is the electron density of a π bond?
choices: On the axis between the nuclei
Above and below the bond axis
pool.hint: π bonds come from p orbitals side by side.
pool.explain: Sideways overlap of p orbitals puts the density in two regions, above and below the axis. Both parts are one π bond.

pool.prompt: Which statement about a C=C double bond is correct?
choices: It is one σ bond and one π bond
pool.hint: Only one bond can lie on the axis.
pool.explain: Only one end-on overlap fits on the axis, so a double bond is one σ plus one π.

pool.prompt: An alkane has {n} carbon atoms, formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. How many σ bonds does it have?
pool.hint: Count the C–C links and the C–H bonds; every single bond is one σ.
pool.explain: {=n-1} C–C bonds plus {=2*n+2} C–H bonds gives {=3*n+1} σ bonds and no π bonds.

pool.prompt: How many σ and π bonds are in ethyne, HC≡CH?
pool.hint: Two C–H bonds plus a triple bond. Do not forget the C–H bonds.
pool.explain: Two C–H σ bonds, plus the triple bond's one σ and two π: 3 σ and 2 π.

pool.prompt: An s orbital overlaps a p orbital that points along the bond axis. Which bond forms?
pool.hint: Is the overlap end-on or sideways?
pool.explain: s is a sphere, so any overlap with it is end-on: the s–p overlap gives a σ bond.

pool.prompt: A molecule has {a} single bonds and {b} double bonds, and no triple bonds. How many σ bonds does it have?
pool.hint: Every bond between two atoms, single or double, contains exactly one σ.
pool.explain: Each of the {a} single bonds is one σ, and each of the {b} double bonds also has one σ: {=a+b} σ bonds, plus {b} π.

pool.prompt: Why does ethene decolourise bromine water but ethane does not?
choices: Ethene's π electrons lie off the axis, open to attack by bromine
Ethane has no electrons to share
Ethene's σ bond is weaker than ethane's
pool.hint: Think about where the π electrons are.
pool.explain: The π electrons sit above and below the axis, so the electrophile bromine can reach them and add across C=C. Ethane has only σ bonds, held on the axes.

pool.prompt: One end of ethene is twisted by 90°. What happens to its bonds?
choices: The σ bond is unchanged but the π overlap falls to zero
pool.hint: Which bond looks the same from every angle round the axis?
pool.explain: σ is symmetric round the axis, so it survives. The p orbitals end up at right angles, so the π bond breaks.

visual.caption: σ only, or σ plus π? Ask: is it a single bond, or a double or triple bond?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: bring orbitals together end-on for σ, twist p orbitals into line for π, twist ethane and ethene, count bonds in propene and weigh π against σ.
